title: Psalm 51:1–19
context: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet went to him after Bathsheba. The king pleads for mercy, confesses native and actual sin, asks for a clean heart and the Spirit’s presence, and widens the prayer to Zion.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What older interpreters in each camp said about mercy that blots out, a clean heart created, and a contrite spirit God will not despise.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Create—Work in me an holy frame of heart, whereby my inward filth may be purged away. Right—Heb. firm or constant, that my resolution may be fixed and unmoveable. Spirit—Temper or disposition of soul. The joy—The comfortable sense of thy saving grace, promised and vouchsafed to me, both for my present and everlasting salvation. Free—Or, ingenuous, or liberal, or princely… a spirit, which may free me from the bondage of sin, and enable me chearfully to run the way of God's precepts.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Ps 51:10, 12)

reformed.quote: Create in me a clean heart, O God! In the previous part of the psalm David has been praying for pardon. He now requests that the grace of the Spirit… might be restored to him… By employing the term create, he expresses his persuasion that nothing less than a miracle could effect his reformation, and emphatically declares that repentance is the gift of God. The Sophists grant the necessity of the aids of the Spirit… but by assigning a middle place to the free will of man, they rob God of a great part of his glory.

verses.text: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions.
verses.arminianNotes:
Have mercy—according to steadfast love and abundant mercy blot out transgressions. Wesley heard lovingkindness and the multitude of tender mercies as the ground of the plea after Nathan exposed David. The king does not bargain; he begs blot-out.

Mercy is true and must be sought. Grace that can blot also summons confession. David’s aggravated sin does not undo the invitation to ask; it deepens the need for rich mercy received.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: David begins by praying for pardon with unwonted earnestness—ordinary kindness would not suffice for so great a sinner. He piles loving-kindness and multitude of compassions because the stain felt deep.

Pardon is God’s work according to His compassions, not David’s worth. The plea rests on who God is. Common confession: blot out is needed; neither camp softens Bathsheba’s aftermath.
verses.keyContrast: Both plead rich mercy to blot out. Arminians stress sincere petition that must still be made; Reformed commentators emphasize that only the multitude of God’s compassions can cover such guilt.

verses.text: Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: cleanse me a leprous creature by grace and by the blood signified in ceremonial washings. Filth is inward; washing must go through.

The request is earnest cooperation with grace that washes. David does not scrub himself into pardon; he asks God to wash—and means it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: multiply to wash me—the stain felt deep, needing multiplied washing. Sin pollutes; remission is aptly compared to washing. The more aggravated the sin, the more earnest the desire for deliverance from terror of conscience.

Only God can wash away sin. Both readings hold: thorough cleansing, not a light rinse.

verses.text: For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me.
verses.arminianNotes:
I know my transgressions; my sin is constantly before me. Wesley: acknowledge—confession that keeps the sin in view rather than burying it. Honesty before God is the doorway of mercy.

Knowledge here is owning, not mere data. Grace enables confession that can still be refused in self-excuse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he is subjected to constant anguish that only reconciliation relieves. Prayer did not proceed from dissimulation; many praise grace who never felt bitterness of divine displeasure. He knows inwardly with keenest anguish.

True penitents are wounded and restless until mercy is assured. Both agree: sin before the eyes; no shrug.

verses.text: Against you, and you only, I have sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight, so you may be proved right when you speak, and justified when you judge.
verses.arminianNotes:
Against you, and you only, I have sinned—evil in your sight—so you may be justified. Wesley: comparatively: nothing more grievous than sin against God; severities will glorify His justice, not blemish it.

Guilt before the Judge is primary even when neighbors were wronged. The confession does not erase Uriah; it ranks the offense rightly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: whether the world pardons or not, God is the Judge; conscience hails him to that bar. Cited in Romans 3: God’s righteousness stands even in human sin. David charges himself and justifies God.

Acquittal among men cannot quiet an accusing conscience. God justified in judgment.

verses.text: Behold, I was born in iniquity. My mother conceived me in sin.
verses.arminianNotes:
Brought forth in iniquity; conceived in sin. Wesley: the filthy stream leads to a corrupt fountain—this crime the fruit of a vile nature still ready to sin as occasion offers.

Original corruption is earnest and aggravates guilt; it does not excuse the adultery. Nature’s bent is confessed so that grace’s need is plain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: not one sin only—born in iniquity, nature entirely depraved. He aggravates guilt, not excuses it. Against Pelagius: sin is hereditary disease, not mere imitation. Corruption extends to every part of the soul.

Original sin is confessed to deepen need of new creation. We are not blank slates.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess native corruption behind the crime. Arminians stress that inherited bent still leaves the act responsible and grace resistible in response; Reformed interpreters stress total native depravity that only sovereign grace can remake.

verses.text: Behold, you desire truth in the inward parts. You teach me wisdom in the inmost place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: uprightness God requires; original corruption and actual sin both contradict that holy will and the knowledge written in the heart.

God teaches wisdom inwardly—truth is not only outward law. The heart can be taught; neglect of that teaching worsens the fall.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: God desires truth in the inward parts—secret as well as gross sins displease Him. David cannot plead ignorance; wisdom was closely brought home. Privilege aggravated the offense.

Inward truth is God’s delight and gift. Agreed: heart-deep honesty, not costume piety.

verses.text: Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean. Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.
verses.arminianNotes:
Purge with hyssop; wash—whiter than snow. Wesley: as lepers were purified by appointed rites, cleanse me by grace and by Christ’s blood those rites signified.

Cleansing is authentic and available to the contrite who ask. Ceremonial shadow points to blood that actually cleanses.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he alludes to legal rites as seals of grace, not trust in the symbol. He asks God to accomplish what the rites signified. The Spirit sprinkles the conscience with Christ’s blood.

Atonement is God’s application of Christ’s satisfaction. Whiter than snow is gift.

verses.text: Let me hear joy and gladness, that the bones which you have broken may rejoice.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joy and gladness; bones you have broken rejoice. Wesley: by the Spirit seal pardon on the conscience; the wounded heart comforted.

Joy is restoration of sensed grace, sought and received. Broken bones name discipline that mercy can reverse into praise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: joy of the Lord reanimates; it comes by hearing the word that pardons. No solid peace except reposing on God’s promises. Bones broken = extreme grief under displeasure.

Assurance grows as God speaks peace. Joy returns after the breaking.

verses.text: Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all of my iniquities.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hide your face from my sins; blot out all iniquities. Parallel to v. 1—pardon reiterated. Wesley’s silence on the verse still fits the blot-out theme: remove the record from sight.

Hide and blot are requests faith keeps making until peace settles. Grace invites the ask.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: hide face from sins = pardoning; blot out explains it. Justification as God’s voluntary forgetting of iniquities. Reiteration shows depth of anxiety for a hard-won favor.

Free pardon cleanses completely. Both hear: no leftover ledger with God.

verses.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Create a clean heart; renew a right spirit. Wesley: work an holy frame that purges inward filth; firm, constant resolution; temper of soul fixed and unmoveable.

Create names God’s work; renew names a spirit that must be kept steadfast. Grace that creates also calls for a fixed will cooperating with the Spirit.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he moves from pardon to sanctification. Create expresses that nothing less than a miracle reforms; repentance is God’s gift. Sophists who leave a middle free will rob God of glory. Renew a right spirit—restoration after fall is still creation-grace.

Clean heart is new creation, not self-rehab. God must make the heart clean.
verses.keyContrast: Both ask God to create a clean heart. Arminians hear creating grace that renews a spirit the believer must keep steadfast; Reformed interpreters hear new-creation grace that leaves no middle free will to share the glory.

verses.text: Don’t throw me from your presence, and don’t take your Holy Spirit from me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Cast me not away; take your Holy Spirit from me. Fear of exile from presence after gross fall. Wesley leaves the verse terse; the plea is retention of the Spirit’s presence.

The Spirit can be grieved and the sense of presence lost; the prayer treats that loss as danger for a believer who has fallen hard.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: Spirit not altogether taken—gifts obscured, not reprobate mind. Elect may fear loss yet hold that grace is incorruptible seed. Against those who say mortal sin alienates the elect entirely.

Cast-away language is the saint’s fear; perseverance holds underneath. Dread of Spirit withdrawn is holy.
verses.keyContrast: Both fear loss of God’s presence after sin. Arminians typically treat the danger as true for a true believer who may finally fall; Reformed readers commonly treat the fear as means while denying final loss of the Spirit in the elect.

verses.text: Restore to me the joy of your salvation. Uphold me with a willing spirit.
verses.arminianNotes:
Restore joy of salvation; uphold with willing spirit. Wesley: comfortable sense of saving grace; free/ingenuous spirit opposed to base servile spirit in his wicked practices—freedom from bondage of sin to run God’s precepts.

Joy restored and a willing spirit upheld—grace that frees for cheerful obedience, not forced drudgery.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: grief remains until peace with God. Free spirit = free and cheerful, not enslaved by guilt; some hear princely courage for kingship. Either way, divine grace alone recovers it.

Joy of salvation is restored gift. Willing spirit is not self-generated pep.

verses.text: Then I will teach transgressors your ways. Sinners will be converted to you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Then teach transgressors; sinners return. Mercy received becomes mission. Wesley’s economy: restored joy overflows into teaching that others may convert.

Teaching and return are aims—grace that saved David aims at others’ turning, which they must still do.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: gratitude constrains helping others into the same grace. He speaks sanguinely of converting others; we forget God can crown such attempts.

Recovered saints become instruments. Pardon fuels witness.

verses.text: Deliver me from the guilt of bloodshed, O God, the God of my salvation. My tongue will sing aloud of your righteousness.
verses.arminianNotes:
Deliver from bloodguiltiness; tongue sings righteousness. Wesley: righteousness = clemency and goodness. Bloodguilt names Uriah and more.

Deliverance from blood-guilt is begged from the God of salvation; praise follows mercy received.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: bloods may mean capital guilt/death-sentence felt; he celebrates God’s righteousness as faithfulness to promise and help. The God of my salvation—trembling yet trusting.

Only mercy clears murder’s stain before heaven. Both see: bloodguilt is not minimized.

verses.text: Lord, open my lips. My mouth will declare your praise.
verses.arminianNotes:
Open my lips; mouth declares praise. Wesley: lips shut with shame and grief. Praise needs God to open what shame closed.

Praise is enabled response—God opens; the mouth then actually declares.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: God afford matter of praise; mouth shut until pardon extends. New song after mercy—not mere eloquence tips.

Praise is answer to grace. Undisputed: shame-closed lips need God.

verses.text: For you don’t delight in sacrifice, or else I would give it. You have no pleasure in burnt offering.
verses.arminianNotes:
You don’t delight in sacrifice, or else I would give it. Wesley: not absolute denial of sacrifice, but these crimes not expiated by any ritual offering.

No bargain of bulls for adultery and murder; mercy and contrition, not payment theater.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: confidence of pardon though he brings no compensation—relies on riches of mercy. Against those who treat sacrifices as purchase price; rites point to Christ, not self-redemption.

Reconciliation is a free gift. No dispute here: burnt offering cannot buy this clean.

verses.text: The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.
verses.arminianNotes:
Broken spirit; contrite heart God will not despise. Wesley: more value than many sacrifices.

Contrition is the offering God receives—humility that can be presented or withheld; grace softens what pride resists.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: sacrifices of God = broken spirit enough without pretended satisfaction. Broken spirit emptied of vain-glorious confidence; contrite heart has no dealings on exchange. Does not exclude faith; shuts out merit.

Penitence is not a wage but the empty hand. God does not despise the crushed heart.
verses.keyContrast: Both prize a broken, contrite heart over ritual. Arminians emphasize sincere contrition grace enables and requires; Reformed commentators typically emphasize contrition as emptied of merit, resting on free mercy alone.

verses.text: Do well in your good pleasure to Zion. Build the walls of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Do good to Zion; build Jerusalem’s walls. Wesley: free rich mercy; perfect the city and especially the temple despite my sins.

Personal pardon widens into prayer for the people—David’s fall must not ruin Zion; he intercedes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: from private prayer to the Church—he had nearly ruined it by his fall. Restores by free good pleasure, not others’ righteousness. God builds the spiritual temple.

Church’s standing is God’s good pleasure. Zion on the penitent’s lips.

verses.text: Then you will delight in the sacrifices of righteousness, in burnt offerings and in whole burnt offerings. Then they will offer bulls on your altar.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: then God pleased with sacrifices of righteousness. Order: mercy and contrition first; public worship gladly follows.

Restored fellowship renews right offering—not bribes, but grateful obedience in the assembly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: sacrifices of righteousness = warrantable, according to commandment, with reference to their proper end. Not empty form. Thanksgiving joins heart disposition to solemn worship.

Accepted offerings flow from prior mercy. Both affirm: altar after blot-out.
